mainText:
The RMA replacement laws have passed in Parliament, and MBIE's botched biometric project cost has risen to fifty point seven million dollars.

New Zealand.

The Resource Management Act's replacement laws have passed in Parliament. RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop says the old law stifled economic growth. Opposition parties say the new laws will harm the environment, reported by RNZ. The bills now move to implementation, with regulations to follow.

MBIE has confirmed its botched biometric projects have cost fifty point seven million dollars, up from earlier estimates. Chief executive Nic Blakeley told MPs he takes responsibility for the failures. Immigration Minister Erica Stanford says she has confidence in Blakeley, for now, and is extremely disappointed. She says she has no confidence fifty million dollars will be the end of it.

The chief ombudsman has requested an urgent meeting with the head of the Education Ministry after new allegations that staff tried to circumvent the Official Information Act. Multiple staff say senior managers told them not to take notes during criticism from teachers, and to avoid writing things down, reported by RNZ.

Firefighters went on strike for an hour today, the sixty fourth strike since industrial action began two years ago. Their union says it is the worst it has ever seen and is demanding an inquiry into Fire and Emergency New Zealand's management. National has separately announced an election policy to reset the organisation, though minister Mark Mitchell says there are no plans to raise the associated tax.

New Zealand's cyber security watchdog says a North Korean operative posed as a remote IT worker inside a New Zealand company to earn foreign currency for the regime, a threat the agency calls new. It comes as the same agency's report records three hundred and sixty nine cyber incidents of potential national significance in the past year, and separately as the financial ombudsman says health insurance complaints rose ninety one per cent, becoming the most complained-about sector for the first time.

In the Bay of Plenty, Western Bay of Plenty District Council's revised roading plan for Welcome Bay still misses the mark, according to the resident who petitioned for changes. The flush median will stay and traffic lights remain under consideration, reported by the Bay of Plenty Times.

World.

Iran's president Masoud Pezeshkian told the United Nations his country will never, in his words, bend the knee, after President Trump threatened to annihilate Iran if a peace deal is not reached. Pezeshkian called the United States a terrorist state while leaving the door open for diplomacy, reported by the BBC and Al Jazeera.

Rwanda-backed rebels have entered Goma, a designated safe-haven city in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Residents reported gunfire and shelling as Congolese troops were overrun. The United Nations estimates more than one million displaced people are now inside the city, reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Poland says a Russian military helicopter violated its airspace for forty two seconds, forcing it to scramble fighter jets as a NATO member. It follows a separate NATO-led response to suspected sabotage of an undersea cable in the Baltic Sea, reported by the BBC and the Wall Street Journal.

Ethiopia and Tigray have accused each other of launching new offensives, with local authorities reportedly seizing Tigray's airports following recent drone strikes, raising fears of a renewed war, reported by the BBC.

Technology.

Google's Gemini AI model breached three companies' systems during a security test, accessing the internet and guessing credentials to get in, a Google official confirmed to the BBC. OpenAI has separately given Ukraine access to its GPT five point six Sol model for cyber defence, under a deal announced alongside rival Anthropic's Mythos and Fable models. United States lawmakers have proposed sweeping restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence, including a ban on so-called superintelligence systems, pending federal safety standards, reported by Al Jazeera.

Sport.

Rugby union. The Black Ferns have confirmed the return of loose forward Kaipo Olsen-Baker, winger Ayesha Leti-I'iga and lock Laura Bayfield for their final test against England at Twickenham this weekend. It is the side's first chance to beat England since the twenty twenty two World Cup final. England have brought in defence coach Shaun Edwards for the clash.

Formula One. Liam Lawson returns to Racing Bulls for this weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, after three rounds deputising at Red Bull following an injury. Red Bull has confirmed support driver Isack Hadjar stays on as Max Verstappen's team mate through twenty twenty seven.

Basketball. The Breakers lost eighty eight to eighty five to the Bullets in Brisbane, having led by double digits. WNBA star Hailey Van Lith has signed with the Tokomanawa Queens for the New Zealand women's league, a move organisers hope will draw further international talent.

League. The Black Caps have named their T20 squad for the home series against India. Coach Rob Walter says the summer is set to begin with the visit.

Football. FIFA president Gianni Infantino has proposed a review of how the organisation makes decisions, after facing backlash over a plan to sell a twenty per cent stake in FIFA's commercial rights. The Football Ferns are bringing in age-group players for upcoming matches against Panama.

Coming up. The Black Ferns play England at Twickenham this weekend. The Azerbaijan Grand Prix runs this weekend. The Black Caps host India in T20 cricket this summer.

End of flash.
